item.title: Act on risks, PRB urged
item.description: THE Public Rental Board (PRB) should be responsible for ensuring condemned buildings are secured and no longer occupied, a parliamentary committee has heard. The issue was raised last Friday during submissions by the National Fire Authority (NFA) to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Social Affairs on the Public Health (Amendment) Bill 2026.
item.content:encoded:
THE Public Rental Board (PRB) should be responsible for ensuring condemned buildings are secured and no longer occupied, a parliamentary committee has heard.

The issue was raised last Friday during submissions by the National Fire Authority (NFA) to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Social Affairs on the Public Health (Amendment) Bill 2026.

Opposition MP Ketan Lal questioned what role public health authorities would play in dealing with unsafe structures, citing the condemned PRB flats in Nabua where people continued to enter and occupy the buildings.

“You can still see people hanging around that place,” Mr Lal said.

“It’s unsafe. According to engineers, it’s unsafe. So how will the public health board step in?”

Responding, Ministry of Health WASH coordinator Toga Vosataki said the matter primarily fell under the National Fire Authority’s jurisdiction.

“In that particular case, since the building is clearly in the jurisdiction of NFA, NFA will take lead in not only conducting the investigation but ensuring that it’s cordoned off in such a way that no one can actually come in and start to squat or stay within the facility,” Mr Vosataki said.

He added that the NFA could seek police assistance to remove occupants, while public health authorities would only intervene where occupied dwellings posed a direct health risk.

Government MP Praveen Kumar then questioned who would be liable if a condemned building remained occupied and an accident occurred before demolition.

Mr Vosataki said responsibility rested with the PRB as the owner of the structure.

“I believe that the team from National Fire Authority would agree with me, for that particular scenario, the PRB will be responsible since the structure is theirs, and they should have a plan in place to demolish or repurpose that particular structure,” he said.

He said the PRB should also coordinate with police to prevent people from entering buildings at risk of collapse.

item.title: NFA seeks demolition checks
item.description: THE National Fire Authority (NFA) is calling for mandatory consultation before unsafe buildings are demolished, warning that premature demolition could destroy critical evidence needed for fire investigations. Making a submission to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Social Affairs on the Public Health (Amendment) Bill 2026 last Friday, NFA chief executive officer Sowane Puamau said the autho
item.content:encoded:
THE National Fire Authority (NFA) is calling for mandatory consultation before unsafe buildings are demolished, warning that premature demolition could destroy critical evidence needed for fire investigations.

Making a submission to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Social Affairs on the Public Health (Amendment) Bill 2026 last Friday, NFA chief executive officer Sowane Puamau said the authority was seeking a simple requirement for the Ministry of Health to consult the NFA before ordering the demolition of properties affected by fire.

“The reason why we are bringing this up is so that we don’t mess up with all these things, like the Public Health saying, ‘Destroy that thing’ without consulting us. We have already completed our investigation on that,” Mr Puamau said.

“It’s just a simple consultation with us, just stating that yes, you can go ahead because we’ve already completed our report and it’s already in.”

He said the proposed measure would ensure the NFA was able to carry out its statutory responsibility of determining the cause of fires before evidence was destroyed.

“They cannot order demolition without consulting us, and if we haven’t completed the investigation,” he said.

Mr Puamau acknowledged that some damaged buildings might pose public health risks, but stressed that due process must still be followed.

He added that people could be held accountable if evidence was destroyed before the NFA completed its investigations, underscoring the importance of preserving fire scenes until investigators had finished their work.

item.title: inDepth I Hidden school crisis
item.description: FOR generations, Fiji’s schools have been regarded as safe spaces where children learn, grow and prepare for adulthood. item.content:encoded:
FOR generations, Fiji’s schools have been regarded as safe spaces where children learn, grow and prepare for adulthood. Today, however, educators are confronting a challenge that extends far beyond textbooks and examinations.

Drugs, risky behaviour and a rapidly escalating HIV epidemic among young people are forcing schools to take on an increasingly important role in protecting students — not only from academic failure, but from life-threatening health risks.

That stark reality was laid bare during the School Management Association of Fiji conference in Suva, where National Substance Abuse Advisory Council (NSAAC) acting chief executive Josua Naisele urged school leaders to recognise that they are now on the frontline of one of Fiji’s biggest public health crises.

“This is happening in our schools now,” Mr Naisele told delegates.

“Teachers are on the front line of early detection and referral.”

His presentation painted a picture that was both alarming and urgent.

By the end of 2025, Fiji had recorded 5676 cumulative HIV cases, including 2016 new infections in a single year.

The epidemic is increasingly affecting young people, with HIV cases among children aged 10 to 14 increasing by 892 per cent since 2015 and infections among 15 to 19-year-olds surging by an astonishing 4183 per cent.

The largest number of new infections is now among people aged 20 to 24, while those under 25 account for 58 per cent of all new HIV cases recorded last year.

For school leaders gathered at the conference, those statistics carried a sobering message: the HIV epidemic is no longer something happening elsewhere.

It is affecting students, families and communities connected to Fiji’s schools.

Mr Naisele explained that the country’s drug problem and HIV epidemic are becoming increasingly intertwined.

“Injection drug use is the number one identified HIV transmission route,” he said.

The presentation showed that injecting drug use accounted for 18 per cent of all new HIV infections recorded in Fiji during 2025, with the overlap between injecting drug use and sexual transmission continuing to grow.

Needle sharing remains one of the most efficient ways HIV spreads.

“When people inject drugs and share needles, HIV passes directly through blood. Even microscopic blood residue is enough.”

Mr Naisele also warned that alcohol and drugs impaired judgement, making young people more likely to engage in unprotected sex, accept dangerous risks or become victims of exploitation.

Drug dependence, he said, could also drive vulnerable young people into transactional or survival sex, exposing them not only to HIV but also to sexually transmitted infections, violence and poor access to healthcare.

While methamphetamine has dominated national headlines, Mr Naisele said schools continue to face a range of substance abuse issues.

Cannabis remains the most common drug used by school-age children and is often the first drug they experiment with before progressing to harder substances.

Alcohol is widely accessible and frequently linked to sexual risk-taking and violence during school events and weekends.

Inhalants such as glue and petrol continue to be used by younger secondary and upper primary students, causing serious damage to developing brains while remaining difficult to detect.

Methamphetamine, meanwhile, is emerging rapidly, with injecting already reported among school-age users in Suva through older drug networks.

The presentation also highlighted growing concerns about sexting and online exploitation, noting that young people using drugs face greater risks of sexual exploitation and transactional sex.

Mr Naisele said substance abuse rarely occurred in isolation.

Peer pressure, the desire to fit in, family dysfunction, trauma, abuse, poverty, lack of awareness about HIV, stigma surrounding help-seeking and limited adult supervision all combined to increase children’s vulnerability.

These factors often reinforce one another, creating environments where experimentation can quickly develop into addiction and risky behaviour.

The challenge, he suggested, cannot be solved through enforcement alone.

He said it requires stronger families, better-informed communities and schools that recognise problems before they escalate.

One of the strongest messages from the presentation was that teachers are not expected to become doctors or investigators.

item.title: Court to set meth trial date
item.description: THE High Court in Suva will set a trial date for two police officers and two civilians charged with methamphetamine-related offences when the matter is recalled in three months. Police officers Sevuloni Lubi, 43, and Ratu Lote Lewaivanua, 32, together with civilians Eroni Kitanamati Bati, 37, and Alipate Matadigo, appeared before Justice Daniel Goundar for a pre-trial conference last Friday.
item.content:encoded:
THE High Court in Suva will set a trial date for two police officers and two civilians charged with methamphetamine-related offences when the matter is recalled in three months.

Police officers Sevuloni Lubi, 43, and Ratu Lote Lewaivanua, 32, together with civilians Eroni Kitanamati Bati, 37, and Alipate Matadigo, appeared before Justice Daniel Goundar for a pre-trial conference last Friday.

The four are charged in relation to the alleged importation and possession of 4.7 kilograms of liquid methamphetamine in 2025.

Justice Goundar directed the men’s lawyers to resolve all outstanding litigation issues, including any representations relating to the charges, before the matter is recalled on November 6.

Senior State lawyer Eoghn Samisoni informed the court that the prosecution would not rely on the accused men’s caution interviews at trial because they contained no admissions.

Sevuloni Lubi outside the High Court in Suva on Friday.

Main picture: Civilians Alipate Matadigo (front) and Eroni Bati (white shirt) leave the High Court in Suva last Friday. n Inset: Ratu Lote Lewaivanua. Pictures: ANDREW NAIDU

item.title: Strength through struggles
item.description: FROM growing up in a broken family to overcoming bullying, body shaming and the challenges of single motherhood, Raksha Radhika Malik believes every setback has prepared her for a bigger purpose. The 2026 Miss India South Pacific Fiji contestant says the pageant is more than a beauty competition — it is an opportunity to inspire women to believe in themselves, no matter their circumstances.
item.content:encoded:
FROM growing up in a broken family to overcoming bullying, body shaming and the challenges of single motherhood, Raksha Radhika Malik believes every setback has prepared her for a bigger purpose.

The 2026 Miss India South Pacific Fiji contestant says the pageant is more than a beauty competition — it is an opportunity to inspire women to believe in themselves, no matter their circumstances.

Raised by her father and his family after her parents separated when she was just one years old, Ms Malik said she learnt resilience from an early age.

“I have faced bullying on social media, body shaming, stress and many taunts because I come from a middle-class family,” she said.

“There was a time when I even gave up on my life, but my dad gave me hope to live again.

“Today I want to show everyone that no matter what we go through, life must go on. Giving up is not an option.”

Originally from Koronubu, Ba, Ms Malik attended Natawa Primary School, Koronubu Sanatan Primary School, AD Patel College and Khalsa College before furthering her studies at the University of the South Pacific and the University of Fiji.

Now a marketing professional, entrepreneur and content creator, she left her job with the Ministry of Education to work from home so she could spend more time raising her four-year-old son.

“My son is my biggest motivation. Motherhood is not the end of my story; it is the beginning of my greatest chapter.”

A former Miss Ba Farmers Queen (2017) and passionate netball player, Ms Malik hopes her journey will encourage more women to become financially independent.

“It’s time for women to wake up, get educated, work, earn and stand on their own feet so no one can point fingers at us.

“We should be independent, build our own homes and live freely with a smile on our faces.”

She credits her father, Satendra Malik, her aunt Sunil Lata, her grandfather Shailendra Malik for shaping the woman she is today.

“We all make mistakes, but we can also correct them. Everyone deserves a chance to change and live a happy life.”

Raksha Radhika Malik with her son Riddhish Divyansh Kumar. Picture: SUPPLIED

item.title: Remittances soar – Central bank records $725m in five months
item.description: CUMULATIVE inward remittances to Fiji for the first five months of this year reached $725.5m, marking a 25 per cent comparted to the same period last year. According to the Reserve Bank of Fiji (RBF), remittance inflows have remained “exceptionally resilient” despite heightened global economic uncertainty, and continued to provide important support to household incomes, foreign exchange earnings a
item.content:encoded:
CUMULATIVE inward remittances to Fiji for the first five months of this year reached $725.5m, marking a 25 per cent comparted to the same period last year.

According to the Reserve Bank of Fiji (RBF), remittance inflows have remained “exceptionally resilient” despite heightened global economic uncertainty, and continued to provide important support to household incomes, foreign exchange earnings and the broader economy.

RBF Governor Ariff Ali said their assessment was that the level of remittances was increasingly being supported by a structural shift rather than solely post-pandemic conditions.

He said those included a larger and more established Fijian diaspora, continued participation in overseas employment schemes such as Australia’s Pacific Australia Mobility (PALM) program and New Zealand’s Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) scheme, and improved access to digital and fintech-based remittance services.

He added ongoing efforts by remittance service providers to reduce transaction costs and expand market reach had also supported the stronger inflows.

“At the same time, remittance growth has moderated from the exceptionally high rates recorded during and immediately after the pandemic period,” Mr Ali told this newspaper.

“Annual growth peaked at 23.1 per cent in 2022 before easing to 2.6 per cent in 2025, indicating that while the remittance base has become significantly larger, growth rates are normalising.

“While it is too early to conclude that remittance inflows have reached a permanent new normal, the evidence suggests that the baseline level of remittances has shifted higher than it was before the pandemic, supported by enduring structural factors.”

However, Mr Ali said the pace of future growth would continue to depend on labour market conditions, migration trends and economic performance in key source countries.

In its June economic review, the central bank said remittances continued to be strong, rising 30.5 per cent to $358.1m cumulative to April on a net basis.

item.title: Fiji Sea Salt producer wins national SME award
item.description: VIANI-based House of Salt – the producers of Fiji Sea Salt and organic wellness goods on Vanua Levu walked away with the National SME of the Year award at the FDB National SME of the Year Awards 2025. The award recognises an SME that has demonstrated outstanding business performance, robust innovation, strong leadership and exceptional growth potential, with the capacity to transition into a major
item.content:encoded:
VIANI-based House of Salt – the producers of Fiji Sea Salt and organic wellness goods on Vanua Levu walked away with the National SME of the Year award at the FDB National SME of the Year Awards 2025.

The award recognises an SME that has demonstrated outstanding business performance, robust innovation, strong leadership and exceptional growth potential, with the capacity to transition into a major corporate enterprise in the years ahead.

House of Salt also won the Sustainable SME of the Year award.

House of Salt owner and director Jone Waitaiti winning both awards meant a lot to the business and to their operations.

“We have been recognised as sustainable because that is always what we try to be at the House of Salt and that is to be sustainable,” Mr Waitaiti told this newspaper.

“We have no waste in our salt production, zero waste.”

Business partner and fiancée Jannette Smith joined her partner in acknowledging their team back at Viani in Cakaudrove for their hard work.

“I want to thank our team for working so hard, coming to us day and night to support us, support family, support the community. I want to thank also my own families for always pushing us forward, also giving us the encouragement to always be there,” Ms Smith said after the win last Friday.

-Best Agri-Business SME of the Year: Avishay Singh of Sahil’s Party Ice and Frozen Supplies

-Sustainable SME of the Year – House of Salt

-Emerging Entrepreneur of the Year – Leone Vulaca Prosthetic and Orthotic Centre

-Women Entrepreneur of the Year – Dr Marilyn Cornelius of Alchemus Prime

-Youth Entrepreneur of the Year- Tanisha Lal of NailedIt

-Best Businessperson of the Year – Apakuki Nalawa of Resonance Entertainment

-Best Cooperative SME of the Year – Lavena Coastal Walk Eco-Tourism Cooperative Limited

-Best Maritime SME of the Year – Krishneel Deo of Delaivuna Farm Fresh Eggs.

FDB chief executive officer Filimone Waqabaca said there were strong responses this year from SMEs with 145 businesses submitting more than 300 applications across eight award categories.

“These numbers tell us something very encouraging. They tell us that entrepreneurship in Fiji is alive and well. They tell us that businesses are investing, growing, innovating and looking beyond today’s challenges towards tomorrow’s opportunities,” Mr Waqabaca said.

He said applications were received from agriculture, fisheries, manufacturing, tourism, renewable energy, technology, retail, food processing, and many other sectors.

He added there were also strong participation from women entrepreneurs, youth-led businesses, cooperatives and enterprises operating in rural and maritime communities.

“It shows that opportunities throughout Fiji – not only in our towns and cities – but in every community where people have the courage to pursue an idea and make it grow.”

item.title: Report vulnerable people – minister
item.description: SOCIAL media users are being encouraged to report vulnerable people seen on the streets instead of making their stories go viral online. The call was made by Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran following recent viral social media videos showing elderly people begging in the Western Division, which prompted concerns about whether the ministry was responding to such cases.
item.content:encoded:
SOCIAL media users are being encouraged to report vulnerable people seen on the streets instead of making their stories go viral online.

The call was made by Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran following recent viral social media videos showing elderly people begging in the Western Division, which prompted concerns about whether the ministry was responding to such cases.

Speaking to The Fiji Times, Ms Kiran said the ministry investigated the cases that had gained attention online and found those involved were already receiving some form of assistance.

“In one case, an elderly woman was renting a home, was being supported by the Muslim League women’s group and also had relatives providing assistance,” she said. In another case in Lautoka, Ms Kiran said the elderly woman told the ministry she was unaware a video of her had been shared widely on social media.

“The woman said her children supported her from time to time and that social welfare assistance for her grandchildren had already been approved.”

Ms Kiran said the portrayal of the cases on social media did not reflect the full circumstances.

She said vulnerable people, particularly older persons, could have complex situations, including mental health conditions or dementia, and sharing their images online without consent was undignified.

“So I am calling on the members of the public who encounter older people, children, young women or anyone appearing vulnerable on the streets to report them to the ministry. We have officers who assess each case and work to ensure those individuals receive appropriate support.”

She said people could contact the ministry through its toll-free helpline, 1561, to report cases requiring assistance.

According to Ms Kiran, the ministry regularly assists vulnerable people by reconnecting some with their families, while others, including those living with dementia, may return to the streets because they view it as part of their social life.

She said the ministry was also reminding families of their responsibility to provide dignified care and protection for elderly relatives, adding that it did not want to resort to taking action against families for neglect.
